name: Wendy Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the die-cutting and folder-gluer line at Hartley Cartons, which makes boxes for cereal and biscuits. I start at seven, check the colour on the first sheets, set the cutting die and then keep the glue and the stack count right for eight hours. I'm the shift lead, so I also settle arguments about who takes the late job. By Friday my hands are tired and my mind is clear.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy about the work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A good run, where the boxes come off square and nobody has to stop the line. And teaching. I've trained eleven people on this machine, and two of them now run their own shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's helpful in some places and mostly noise elsewhere. At work I'd say, use it for the boring stuff and check it. To friends I'd say it won't change my life, and probably not theirs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us I'm relaxed about it. I've been using a chatbot now and then to word emails to customers and to make sense of the glue supplier's data sheets. It's saved me a bit of time, and that's about all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job, and use the chatbot when it makes sense. I'd keep our savings as they are, and Graham and I would carry on with our plan to retire around 62. I'd keep training the new starter, Nadia, on the gluer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. There's nothing about this that threatens how I earn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has anything already changed at Hartley because of AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The planner started using one to draft the production schedules. It still takes her as long to correct it as it would have taken to write. So we've not got anywhere yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would that change how you spend your money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. We've got a decent cushion and we spend like we always did. A boat would be a nice idea, but nobody's made that decision.

It won't change my life, and probably not yours.
think: I'm **relaxed**: it only helps me with emails and glue data sheets.
Nothing about this threatens how I earn.
do: Use the chatbot when it makes sense for customer **emails**.
Keep our savings as they are and plan to **retire** around 62.
Keep training Nadia on the gluer.
feel: **Calm**, because nothing here threatens how I earn.
S0.quote: I've been using a chatbot now and then to word emails to customers and to make sense of the glue supplier's data sheets.
fieldNote: She uses AI **lightly** and sees little gain from it so far.
Money and retirement date make calm genuine.
Plain, pragmatic voice with small workplace stories.

steps.text: Keep running the folder-gluer line and training Nadia
Use the chatbot for customer emails and glue data sheets

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office goes first. Our planner, the buyer who orders board, the customer service desk. A lot of their day is exactly what these programs do well, and I'd expect Hartley to hire fewer people there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm a little uneasy. The floor changes slower, but when the firm saves in the office it starts looking at the floor too. I think it shifts the mood. Our shift lead jobs are safe for now, but nothing's forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try more of the AI tools once the planner shows they work. I'd ask the firm if they'd pay for a short course on the new machine software. I'd also nudge my savings up a little, just so there's more of a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's not mine yet, but it's at the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Hartley would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cheryl at the customer desk is 47 and her husband's been laid off. If her job goes, they're in trouble. I'd tell her to ask the firm now what they plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try anything new to stay ahead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm open to it once it's proven. I won't be first, but I won't be last either.

I'd expect Hartley to hire fewer people there.
think: When the firm saves in the office, it starts looking at the **floor** too.

do: Try more AI tools once the planner shows they **work**.

feel: **Uneasy**; it's not mine yet, but it's at the door.
S1.quote: I'm open to it once it's proven. I won't be first, but I won't be last either.
fieldNote: Her **steady** profile shows: open once proven, not first.
Concern is for named colleagues like Cheryl at the customer desk.
Her own role is secure, so the unease is mild.

steps.text: Ask the firm to pay for a machine-software course
Try the planner's AI scheduling tool once it works
Raise the monthly savings amount by a few hundred

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a lot too fast. Two years isn't long enough for anyone to retrain, and I'd say the government needs to step in with a plan. I'd be saying it at work and I'd tell my MP.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, the office jobs go in 2028 and then a robot to feed the gluer and stack boxes shows up in 2031. I'd be 63 then and it's the point my retirement plan collides with the robots. I could probably last, but I wouldn't count on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring my retirement forward to 61 if I could afford it. I'd ask the firm what they plan, and put my name down for any robot-cell course. And I'd cut some spending, the holiday and the new kitchen, to build more cushion. I'd talk to Graham, who's a joiner, about whether his work would last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd have savings, but it would still feel like the ground moved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the firm in the first month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for the written plan for the shop floor and the dates. And whether people over 55 can leave early on decent terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think the firm would do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The firm would keep a few of us to supervise, I think, and let the others go. I'd want to be in the group that chooses to leave, not the group that's told to.

I'd tell my MP the government must step in with a plan.
think: The office goes in 2028 and the **robots** reach my gluer by 2031.
That's right where my retirement plan collides with them.
do: Bring my retirement forward to **61** if I can afford it.
Put my name down for any robot-cell course.
Cut the holiday and the new kitchen to build more **cushion**.
feel: **Anxious**; I'd have savings, but it would feel like the ground moved.
S2.quote: I'd want to be in the group that chooses to leave, not the group that's told to.
fieldNote: She wants **choice** over her exit, which is her key concern.
Practical: courses, a written plan, and spending cuts.
Her partner Graham's joinery work is a second thing to check.

steps.text: Ask HR whether over-55s can leave early on decent terms
Put my name down for any robot-cell course
Cancel the holiday and the kitchen to add to the cushion
Write to my MP asking for a plan for factory workers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is workable if everyone starts now. At work I'd push for the firm to put out a plan and for the younger ones to take whatever training is on offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quietly, I think I'd get through this one. Robots arrive in 2034 and I'd be 66, well retired. It's more the next generation, like Nadia, who'll be there. I'd feel a duty to teach her what the machine really does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running the line, aim to stop at 62, and spend the last years teaching Nadia and another operator what I know. I'd put money into the house, the roof and windows, so we're not paying for repairs on a pension. And I'd keep an eye on Graham's work, in case we need to change plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little uneasy, but better. I could see it coming and there's time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Graham and my daughter Zara. She's in marketing and thinks it's going to hit her sooner than me. I'd tell her to be the person who knows how to use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the firm that it's cheaper to train now than hire again later.

S3.quote: I'd tell the firm that it's cheaper to train now than hire again later.
fieldNote: Time converts her worry into **teaching** and home repairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years gives everyone a fair chance. I'd say it's enough for unions, firms and government to put something proper together. I'd feel good about it, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record it's not my fight by then. I'd have been retired for eight years. I'd think about Zara and Nadia, and whether the next generation finds steady work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work to 62, then do volunteer teaching in the local college's engineering classes. I'd travel with Graham. I'd also put a small amount aside for Zara's retraining, if she needs it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It doesn't threaten me, and I can plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for Hartley?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want it still making boxes, with people who know their craft working next to machines. And I'd want the people there to be treated fairly when things change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think people will use the time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is plenty of time if people use it. The worry is that most won't.

say: Ten years gives everyone a **fair chance** if unions, firms and government plan together.
I'd feel good about it, honestly.
think: I'd be **retired** for eight years by 2036, so it isn't my fight.
I'd think about Zara and Nadia finding steady work.
do: Work to **62**, then volunteer in the college's engineering classes.
Put a small amount aside for Zara's **retraining**.
feel: **Calm**; it doesn't threaten me, and I can plan.
S4.quote: Ten years is plenty of time if people use it. The worry is that most won't.
fieldNote: Ten years gives her a calm, **teaching** retirement.
Her honest concern is that most people will waste the time.
Her secure money and age make this her calmest picture.

steps.text: Work until 62, then retire with Graham
Volunteer in the college's engineering classes after I stop
Set aside money for Zara's possible retraining

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there'd be no time for the plan I've made. What would help is a clear plan from the firm and decent terms for the over-55s.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: No, only that people think a calm person has nothing to worry about. I've got a lot of people I care about on that floor.

headlineQuote: People think a calm person has nothing to worry about. I've got a lot of people I care about on that floor.
portrait: Wendy (**58**, shift lead on a die-cutting and gluing line at a carton plant) is pragmatic and uses a chatbot occasionally.
She has strong savings and a plan to **retire** around 62 with her partner Graham.
She names the office jobs as first in line and worries for colleagues like Cheryl and young Nadia.
Her mood rises to **anxious** only when robots arrive in 2031, right where her retirement plan collides with them.
biggestWorry: The **2028** scenario worries her most because it collides with her retirement plan and leaves no time.
whatWouldHelp: A clear **plan** from the firm and decent early exit terms for the over 55s.
